claim: Transposable elements (TEs) are an important source of genome variability.
source: Transposable elements (TEs) are an important source of genome variability.
evidence: This is a general statement presented in the abstract and introduction, supported by established scientific knowledge about TEs.

claim: TE insertions are associated with changes of expression of many genes known to be targets of rice domestication and breeding.
source: Our data show that TE insertions are associated with changes of expression of many genes known to be targets of rice domestication and breeding.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: An important fraction of TE insertions associated with gene expression changes were already present in the rice wild ancestors.
source: An important fraction of these insertions were already present in the rice wild ancestors, and have been differentially selected in indica and japonica rice populations.
evidence: This is supported by data showing TIP presence in rufipogon/nivara populations presented in the Results section.

claim: TE insertions associated with gene expression changes have been differentially selected in indica and japonica rice populations.
source: An important fraction of these insertions were already present in the rice wild ancestors, and have been differentially selected in indica and japonica rice populations.
evidence: This is supported by PBS analysis and selection statistics presented in the manuscript.

claim: Small changes of expression in signal transduction genes induced by TE insertions accompany the domestication and adaptation of rice populations.
source: Taken together, our results show that small changes of expression in signal transduction genes induced by TE insertions accompany the domestication and adaptation of rice populations.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the data presented throughout the manuscript showing TIP-eQTLs in signal transduction genes.

claim: TEs are a major component of eukaryotic genomes, particularly in plants.
source: Transposable elements (TEs) are a major component of eukaryotic genomes, particularly in plants (Wendel et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wendel et al., 2016.

claim: TEs are a major source of genetic variability due to their ability to move, create mutations by insertion/excision, and amplify in genomes.
source: Their ability to move, creating mutations by insertion/excision, and amplify in genomes – thus generating new copies that provide opportunities for recombination – make them a major source of genetic variability (Tenaillon et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tenaillon et al., 2010.

claim: TEs are considered a major driver of plant genome evolution, both in the wild and under human selection.
source: For this reason, TEs are considered a major driver of plant genome evolution, both in the wild and under human selection (Lisch, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lisch, 2013.

claim: TE insertions and other structural variants have been frequently overlooked when using genome-wide association studies (GWAS) to look for genetic variants linked to interesting phenotypes.
source: TE insertions and other structural variants, however, have been frequently overlooked when using genome-wide association studies (GWAS) to look for genetic variants linked to interesting phenotypes (Voichek and Weigel, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Voichek and Weigel, 2020.

claim: Several GWAS reports have shown that TIPs uncover additional variability linked to phenotypic traits.
source: The recent development of efficient tools to identify transposon insertion polymorphisms (TIPs) (Vendrell-Mir et al., 2019) has allowed the incorporation of TIPs in these analyses, and several GWAS reports have shown that TIPs uncover additional variability linked to phenotypic traits (Akakpo et al., 2020; Domínguez et al., 2020; Castanera et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies (Akakpo et al., 2020; Domínguez et al., 2020; Castanera et al., 2021).

claim: TIPs often explain more phenotypic variance compared to single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs).
source: Interestingly, TIPs often explain more phenotypic variance compared to single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), and can be used for genomic prediction (Vourlaki et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Vourlaki et al., 2022.

claim: TIPs can be used for genomic prediction.
source: Interestingly, TIPs often explain more phenotypic variance compared to single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), and can be used for genomic prediction (Vourlaki et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Vourlaki et al., 2022.

claim: As compared with SNPs, TE insertions are more frequently the causal mutation.
source: The reason for this could be that, as compared with SNPs, TE insertions are more frequently the causal mutation.
evidence: This is presented as a speculative explanation for why TIPs explain more variance.

claim: A major fraction of the mutations linked to crop domestication and breeding are associated with changes of the expression of genes involved in signal transduction.
source: A major fraction of the mutations linked to crop domestication and breeding are associated with changes of the expression of genes involved in signal transduction (Swinnen et al., 2016; Meyer and Purugganan, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Swinnen et al., 2016 and Meyer and Purugganan, 2013.

claim: TEs can alter gene transcription, activating or repressing them, by different means.
source: TEs can alter gene transcription, activating or repressing them, by different means.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by established knowledge about TE mechanisms.

claim: Insertion of TEs within a promoter can interfere with transcription.
source: On the one hand, insertion of TEs within a promoter can interfere with transcription, and the silencing of TEs inserted close to genes can result in repression of gene expression (Wang et al., 2020; Martin et al., 2009; Quadrana, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2020; Martin et al., 2009; Quadrana, 2020.

claim: The silencing of TEs inserted close to genes can result in repression of gene expression.
source: On the one hand, insertion of TEs within a promoter can interfere with transcription, and the silencing of TEs inserted close to genes can result in repression of gene expression (Wang et al., 2020; Martin et al., 2009; Quadrana, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2020; Martin et al., 2009; Quadrana, 2020.

claim: TE insertions can result in gene overexpression.
source: Alternatively, TE insertions can also result in gene overexpression (Tian et al., 2022; Studer et al., 2011), as TEs bring their own transcriptional promoters that can induce expression of neighboring genes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tian et al., 2022 and Studer et al., 2011.

claim: TEs bring their own transcriptional promoters that can induce expression of neighboring genes.
source: Alternatively, TE insertions can also result in gene overexpression (Tian et al., 2022; Studer et al., 2011), as TEs bring their own transcriptional promoters that can induce expression of neighboring genes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tian et al., 2022 and Studer et al., 2011.

claim: LTR retrotransposons contain promoters in their 5′ and 3′ LTRs.
source: This is particularly clear for LTR retrotransposons which contain promoters in their 5′ and 3′ LTRs, and may provide nearby genes with alternative promoters.
evidence: This is established knowledge about LTR retrotransposon structure.

claim: LTR retrotransposons may provide nearby genes with alternative promoters.
source: This is particularly clear for LTR retrotransposons which contain promoters in their 5′ and 3′ LTRs, and may provide nearby genes with alternative promoters.
evidence: This is inferred from the known structure of LTR retrotransposons.

claim: TEs can contain transcription factor-binding sites (TFBS) that can alter the expression of host genes.
source: In addition, TEs can also contain transcription factor-binding sites (TFBS) that can alter the expression of host genes (Rebollo et al., 2012); it has been shown, for example, that miniature inverted-repeat transposable elements (MITEs) have frequently amplified and redistributed TFBS in plant genomes (Morata et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rebollo et al., 2012 and Morata et al., 2018.

claim: Miniature inverted-repeat transposable elements (MITEs) have frequently amplified and redistributed TFBS in plant genomes.
source: In addition, TEs can also contain transcription factor-binding sites (TFBS) that can alter the expression of host genes (Rebollo et al., 2012); it has been shown, for example, that miniature inverted-repeat transposable elements (MITEs) have frequently amplified and redistributed TFBS in plant genomes (Morata et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Morata et al., 2018.

claim: Rice is one of the most important food crops in the world.
source: Rice is one of the most important food crops in the world, and varieties are generally found in two subspecies – Oryza sativa ssp. japonica and ssp. indica.
evidence: This is established knowledge about rice.

claim: Rice varieties are generally found in two subspecies – Oryza sativa ssp. japonica and ssp. indica.
source: Rice is one of the most important food crops in the world, and varieties are generally found in two subspecies – Oryza sativa ssp. japonica and ssp. indica.
evidence: This is established knowledge about rice taxonomy.

claim: Aus varieties appear closely related to indica.
source: Other minor variety groups include aus varieties, which appear closely related to indica, and basmati rice varieties that appear to be a hybrid between ssp. japonica and aus.
evidence: This is established knowledge about rice population structure.

claim: Basmati rice varieties appear to be a hybrid between ssp. japonica and aus.
source: Other minor variety groups include aus varieties, which appear closely related to indica, and basmati rice varieties that appear to be a hybrid between ssp. japonica and aus.
evidence: This is established knowledge about rice population structure.

claim: The study used a recently published transcriptional analysis of 208 rice varieties belonging to the major rice variety groups grown under wet paddy and intermittent drought conditions.
source: We took advantage of a recently published transcriptional analysis of 208 rice varieties belonging to the major rice variety groups grown under wet paddy and intermittent drought conditions (Groen et al., 2020) to perform an expression quantitative trait locus (eQTL) GWAS using TIPs as genetic markers.
evidence: This describes the data source used in the study, citing Groen et al., 2020.

claim: The study performed an expression quantitative trait locus (eQTL) GWAS using TIPs as genetic markers.
source: We took advantage of a recently published transcriptional analysis of 208 rice varieties belonging to the major rice variety groups grown under wet paddy and intermittent drought conditions (Groen et al., 2020) to perform an expression quantitative trait locus (eQTL) GWAS using TIPs as genetic markers.
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: TIPs are frequently associated with changes of expression of rice genes.
source: We show that TIPs are frequently associated with changes of expression of rice genes and that many TIPs altering the expression of regulatory genes have been positively selected in indica and japonica rice subspecies.
evidence: This is a main finding of the study supported by the eQTL mapping data.

claim: Many TIPs altering the expression of regulatory genes have been positively selected in indica and japonica rice subspecies.
source: We show that TIPs are frequently associated with changes of expression of rice genes and that many TIPs altering the expression of regulatory genes have been positively selected in indica and japonica rice subspecies.
evidence: This is a main finding of the study supported by PBS and selection analyses.

claim: The study analyzed an 'indica' dataset for 126 O. sativa ssp. indica and some circum-aus accessions.
source: The data we analyzed consist of an 'indica' dataset for 126 O. sativa ssp. indica and some circum-aus accessions, and 82 'japonica' accessions comprising of O. sativa ssp. japonica and some circum-basmati varieties, described in Groen et al., 2020.
evidence: This describes the dataset composition used in the study.

claim: The study analyzed 82 'japonica' accessions comprising of O. sativa ssp. japonica and some circum-basmati varieties.
source: The data we analyzed consist of an 'indica' dataset for 126 O. sativa ssp. indica and some circum-aus accessions, and 82 'japonica' accessions comprising of O. sativa ssp. japonica and some circum-basmati varieties, described in Groen et al., 2020.
evidence: This describes the dataset composition used in the study.

claim: The study identified 45,050 TIPs using PopoolationTE2.
source: We predicted TIPs using PopoolationTE2 (Kofler et al., 2016), and identified 45,050 TIPs.
evidence: This is a result from the TIP detection analysis.

claim: The TIP genotyping on this dataset has 97.1% sensitivity and 92.2% precision.
source: Using the Minghui MH63 short-read data and assembled genome (Zhang et al., 2016), we estimated the performance of the TIP genotyping on this dataset to have 97.1% sensitivity and 92.2% precision (see methods).
evidence: This is a result from the validation analysis using MH63 genome.

claim: Most of the TIPs detected are DNA transposons (84%).
source: Most of the TIPs detected are DNA transposons (84%), especially MITEs belonging to the Stowaway (24%) and Tourist (20%) superfamilies; LTR retrotransposons make up a minor fraction (9 %).
evidence: This is a result from the TIP classification analysis.

claim: MITEs belonging to the Stowaway superfamily represent 24% of detected TIPs.
source: Most of the TIPs detected are DNA transposons (84%), especially MITEs belonging to the Stowaway (24%) and Tourist (20%) superfamilies; LTR retrotransposons make up a minor fraction (9 %).
evidence: This is a result from the TIP classification analysis.

claim: MITEs belonging to the Tourist superfamily represent 20% of detected TIPs.
source: Most of the TIPs detected are DNA transposons (84%), especially MITEs belonging to the Stowaway (24%) and Tourist (20%) superfamilies; LTR retrotransposons make up a minor fraction (9 %).
evidence: This is a result from the TIP classification analysis.

claim: LTR retrotransposons make up 9% of detected TIPs.
source: Most of the TIPs detected are DNA transposons (84%), especially MITEs belonging to the Stowaway (24%) and Tourist (20%) superfamilies; LTR retrotransposons make up a minor fraction (9 %).
evidence: This is a result from the TIP classification analysis.

claim: 81.3% of TIPs are less than 5 kb away from an annotated gene.
source: The 45,050 TIPs are distributed along the 12 chromosomes and 81.3% of them are less than 5 kb away from an annotated gene (IRGSP RAP-DB gene models).
evidence: This is a result from the genomic distribution analysis of TIPs.

claim: Up to 81.4% of rice genes have a TIP less than 5 kb distant.
source: This results in up to 81.4% of rice genes having a TIP less than 5 kb distant.
evidence: This is a result from the genomic distribution analysis of TIPs.

claim: The study found a total of 563 significant associations between TIPs and gene expression levels in the indica population.
source: We found a total of 563 significant associations between TIPs and gene expression levels in the indica population and 356 in the japonica population (TIP-eQTLs with minor allele frequency (MAF) >3%, false discovery rate [FDR] adjusted p-value <0.05 in at least one replicate) (Figure 1A, B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a main result from the eQTL mapping analysis.

claim: The study found 356 significant associations between TIPs and gene expression levels in the japonica population.
source: We found a total of 563 significant associations between TIPs and gene expression levels in the indica population and 356 in the japonica population (TIP-eQTLs with minor allele frequency (MAF) >3%, false discovery rate [FDR] adjusted p-value <0.05 in at least one replicate) (Figure 1A, B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a main result from the eQTL mapping analysis.

claim: TIP-eQTLs involve 477 genes in indica, representing 3.1% of the expressed genes.
source: These involve 477 and 317 genes, in indica and japonica, respectively, representing 3.1% and 2% of the expressed genes.
evidence: This is a result from the eQTL mapping analysis.

claim: TIP-eQTLs involve 317 genes in japonica, representing 2% of the expressed genes.
source: These involve 477 and 317 genes, in indica and japonica, respectively, representing 3.1% and 2% of the expressed genes.
evidence: This is a result from the eQTL mapping analysis.

claim: The proportion of TE orders found in the significant TIPs did not differ significantly from their representation across the genome.
source: The TIP-eQTLs were related to the different TE types (orders Wicker et al., 2007), and the proportion of TE orders found in the significant TIPs did not differ significantly from their representation across the genome (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a result from the analysis of TE types in TIP-eQTLs, shown in Figure 1C.

claim: For most genes that have an associated TIP, either there is no associated SNP or the TIP explains more expression variance than the associated SNP (~62% of the indica TIP-eQTLs and ~73% of the japonica TIP-eQTLs).
source: For most genes that have an associated TIP, either there is no associated SNP or the TIP explains more expression variance than the associated SNP (~62% of the indica TIP-eQTLs and ~73% of the japonica TIP-eQTLs) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a result from the comparison of TIP and SNP variance explained, shown in Figure 1D.

claim: TIPs uncover genetic associations with changes of expression that are not observed when using SNPs as molecular markers.
source: This demonstrates that TIPs uncover genetic associations with changes of expression that are not observed when using SNPs as molecular markers.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of TIP and SNP eQTL analyses.

claim: SNP-eQTLs are associated to both positive (47%) and negative (53%) effects on gene expression levels.
source: The SNP-eQTLs found in our study are associated to both positive (47%) and negative (53%) effects on gene expression levels, very close to an even distribution.
evidence: This is a result from the analysis of SNP-eQTL effects.

claim: TIPs more frequently have a negative effect (59%) on gene expression.
source: In contrast, TIPs more frequently have a negative effect (59%).
evidence: This is a result from the analysis of TIP-eQTL effects.

claim: TIR/MULEs have close to 50% negative effect on gene expression.
source: The proportion varies among TE superfamilies, with TIR/MULEs being close to 50%, and LTR/Gypsy having the most frequently negative impact on gene expression (67%, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a result from the analysis of TIP-eQTL effects by TE superfamily.

claim: LTR/Gypsy elements have the most frequently negative impact on gene expression (67%).
source: The proportion varies among TE superfamilies, with TIR/MULEs being close to 50%, and LTR/Gypsy having the most frequently negative impact on gene expression (67%, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a result from the analysis of TIP-eQTL effects by TE superfamily.

claim: As compared with SNP-eQTLs, TIP-eQTLs are more frequently the likely causal mutation responsible for the change in expression.
source: This suggests that, as compared with SNP-eQTLs, TIP-eQTLs are more frequently the likely causal mutation responsible for the change in expression, and that the effect of the insertion is more generally negative, in line with recent analyses done in Capsella (Uzunović et al., 2019), especially for long elements such as LTR retrotransposons.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data on effect directionality, supported by citation to Uzunović et al., 2019.

claim: The effect of TE insertion is more generally negative, especially for long elements such as LTR retrotransposons.
source: This suggests that, as compared with SNP-eQTLs, TIP-eQTLs are more frequently the likely causal mutation responsible for the change in expression, and that the effect of the insertion is more generally negative, in line with recent analyses done in Capsella (Uzunović et al., 2019), especially for long elements such as LTR retrotransposons.
evidence: This is supported by data from this study and citation to Uzunović et al., 2019.

claim: SNP-eQTLs are more evenly distributed across the genic region.
source: An analysis of the TIP- and SNP-eQTL location with respect to the associated genes shows that while SNP-eQTLs are more evenly distributed across the genic region (Figure 1F), TIP-eQTLs are over-represented in the 1 kb region upstream of the gene (Figure 1E), which is the region that most frequently contains promoter elements regulating transcription.
evidence: This is a result from the genomic location analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: TIP-eQTLs are over-represented in the 1 kb region upstream of the gene.
source: An analysis of the TIP- and SNP-eQTL location with respect to the associated genes shows that while SNP-eQTLs are more evenly distributed across the genic region (Figure 1F), TIP-eQTLs are over-represented in the 1 kb region upstream of the gene (Figure 1E), which is the region that most frequently contains promoter elements regulating transcription.
evidence: This is a result from the genomic location analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The 1 kb region upstream of the gene most frequently contains promoter elements regulating transcription.
source: An analysis of the TIP- and SNP-eQTL location with respect to the associated genes shows that while SNP-eQTLs are more evenly distributed across the genic region (Figure 1F), TIP-eQTLs are over-represented in the 1 kb region upstream of the gene (Figure 1E), which is the region that most frequently contains promoter elements regulating transcription.
evidence: This is established knowledge about gene regulatory regions.

claim: An important fraction of TIP-eQTLs could be the actual causal mutation inducing expression variation.
source: This suggests that although some TIP-eQTLs could be in linkage disequilibrium with the causal mutation for the change of expression, an important fraction of TIP-eQTLs could be the actual causal mutation inducing expression variation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the enrichment of TIP-eQTLs in upstream regions.

claim: An important fraction of gene expression variation is deleterious.
source: It has been proposed that an important fraction of gene expression variation is deleterious, and therefore, alleles associated with major expression effects should be maintained at lower frequencies (Josephs et al., 2015; Lye et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Josephs et al., 2015 and Lye et al., 2022.

claim: Alleles associated with major expression effects should be maintained at lower frequencies.
source: It has been proposed that an important fraction of gene expression variation is deleterious, and therefore, alleles associated with major expression effects should be maintained at lower frequencies (Josephs et al., 2015; Lye et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Josephs et al., 2015 and Lye et al., 2022.

claim: Low- and high-frequency TIPs (corresponding to rare alleles) show the highest positive or negative effect on the expression of the associated gene.
source: An analysis of the effect size of the different TIP-eQTLs taking into account their frequency in the population shows that, indeed, low- and high-frequency TIPs (corresponding to rare alleles) show the highest positive or negative effect on the expression of the associated gene (Figure 2A–D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from the analysis of effect size vs. frequency shown in Figure 2A-D.

claim: The pattern of rare TIPs showing highest effects is consistent with the rare variant effect.
source: This is consistent with what is described as the rare variant effect (Lye et al., 2022) where rare (and likely deleterious) mutations in a population are associated with greater effects on gene expression in a population.
evidence: This interpretation is supported by citation to Lye et al., 2022.

claim: There is an important overlap of eQTLs between the two different growth conditions (38.5% for indica TIP-eQTLs and 33.2% for japonica TIP-eQTLs).
source: A comparison of TIP-eQTLs associated with changes of expression in the two different growth conditions (wet and drought stress) shows that there is an important overlap of eQTLs between the two environments (38.5% for indica TIP-eQTLs and 33.2% for japonica TIP-eQTLs) (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a result from the comparison of TIP-eQTLs across conditions shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The overlap of TIP-eQTLs between conditions increases to 90% (average of indica and japonica, wet) and 71% (average of indica and japonica, drought stress) when comparing with non-FDR-corrected TIP-eQTLs.
source: Such overlap increases to 90% (average of indica and japonica, wet) and 71% (average of indica and japonica, drought stress) when we compare TIP-eQTLs of one condition with non-FDR-corrected TIP-eQTLs in the other environment (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a result from the comparison using relaxed significance thresholds shown in Figure 2F.

claim: All the associations shared in the two environments had the same effect type on expression (positive or negative).
source: All the associations shared in the two environments had the same effect type on expression (positive or negative).
evidence: This is a result from the comparison of TIP-eQTLs across conditions.

claim: The majority of TIP-eQTLs are general associations with changes of expression in both growth conditions.
source: This result suggests that the majority of TIP-eQTLs are general associations with changes of expression in both growth conditions, and that only a small number of TIP-eQTLs (81 in indica and 78 in japonica) are associated with stress-specific changes of expression.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the high overlap of TIP-eQTLs between conditions.

claim: Only a small number of TIP-eQTLs (81 in indica and 78 in japonica) are associated with stress-specific changes of expression.
source: This result suggests that the majority of TIP-eQTLs are general associations with changes of expression in both growth conditions, and that only a small number of TIP-eQTLs (81 in indica and 78 in japonica) are associated with stress-specific changes of expression.
evidence: This is calculated from the data on condition-specific TIP-eQTLs.

claim: TIP_49046 is associated with a reduction of the expression of the gene synaptotagmin-5 (OsSYT-5).
source: As an example, TIP_49046 is associated with a reduction of the expression of the gene synaptotagmin-5 (OsSYT-5).
evidence: This is a specific example from the TIP-eQTL data.

claim: OsSYT-5 encodes a Ca2+ sensing protein with a C2 domain.
source: OsSYT-5 encodes a Ca2+ sensing protein with a C2 domain, is expressed in both stressed and non-stressed plants, and it has been recently shown that its silencing enhances drought tolerance in rice (Shanmugam et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Shanmugam et al., 2021.

claim: OsSYT-5 is expressed in both stressed and non-stressed plants.
source: OsSYT-5 encodes a Ca2+ sensing protein with a C2 domain, is expressed in both stressed and non-stressed plants, and it has been recently shown that its silencing enhances drought tolerance in rice (Shanmugam et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Shanmugam et al., 2021.

claim: Silencing of OsSYT-5 enhances drought tolerance in rice.
source: OsSYT-5 encodes a Ca2+ sensing protein with a C2 domain, is expressed in both stressed and non-stressed plants, and it has been recently shown that its silencing enhances drought tolerance in rice (Shanmugam et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Shanmugam et al., 2021.

claim: TIP_23764 is associated with an increased expression of the gene encoding the OsSAPK10 ABA-activated protein kinase.
source: Other examples are TIP_23764 and TIP_52367, associated with an increased expression of the gene encoding the OsSAPK10 ABA-activated protein kinase and the S-type euonymus-related lectin gene OsEULS2 in, respectively, two genes known to mediate drought stress in rice (Gao et al., 2022; Lambin et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a specific example from the TIP-eQTL data.

claim: TIP_52367 is associated with an increased expression of the S-type euonymus-related lectin gene OsEULS2.
source: Other examples are TIP_23764 and TIP_52367, associated with an increased expression of the gene encoding the OsSAPK10 ABA-activated protein kinase and the S-type euonymus-related lectin gene OsEULS2 in, respectively, two genes known to mediate drought stress in rice (Gao et al., 2022; Lambin et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a specific example from the TIP-eQTL data.

claim: OsSAPK10 and OsEULS2 are genes known to mediate drought stress in rice.
source: Other examples are TIP_23764 and TIP_52367, associated with an increased expression of the gene encoding the OsSAPK10 ABA-activated protein kinase and the S-type euonymus-related lectin gene OsEULS2 in, respectively, two genes known to mediate drought stress in rice (Gao et al., 2022; Lambin et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gao et al., 2022 and Lambin et al., 2020.

claim: The overlap between indica and japonica TIP-eQTLs is low, with only 90 TIP-eQTLs out of the 563 from indica and 356 from japonica significantly associated with variation of gene expression in both subspecies.
source: Although the overlap of TIPs associated with changes in expression under wet and drought stress conditions is very high, the overlap between indica and japonica TIP-eQTLs is low, and only 90 TIP-eQTLs out of the 563 from indica and 356 from japonica are significantly associated with variation of gene expression in both subspecies (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a result from the comparison of TIP-eQTLs between subspecies shown in Figure 2E.

claim: ~69% of indica and ~60% of japonica TIP-eQTLs appear as subspecies specific when using less-stringent comparison.
source: Even when we make the less-stringent comparison of the TIP-eQTLs of one subspecies with the non-FDR-corrected TIP-eQTLs of the other, as much as ~69% of indica and ~60% of japonica TIP-eQTLs appear as subspecies specific (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a result from the comparison using relaxed significance thresholds shown in Figure 2F.

claim: All common associations between subspecies have the same effect type on expression (positive or negative).
source: Regarding the common associations between subspecies, all of them have the same effect type on expression (positive or negative).
evidence: This is a result from the comparison of TIP-eQTLs between subspecies.

claim: Approximately one-third of the TIPs are only found in one of the two subspecies at MAF >3%.
source: An analysis of the frequencies in indica and japonica of all the TIP-eQTLs described here shows that approximately one-third of the TIPs are only found in one of the two subspecies at MAF >3%, although only 59 (indica) and 21 (japonica) associations correspond to truly species-specific TIPs (completely absent in one of the two subspecies).
evidence: This is a result from the frequency analysis of TIP-eQTLs.

claim: Only 59 (indica) and 21 (japonica) associations correspond to truly species-specific TIPs (completely absent in one of the two subspecies).
source: An analysis of the frequencies in indica and japonica of all the TIP-eQTLs described here shows that approximately one-third of the TIPs are only found in one of the two subspecies at MAF >3%, although only 59 (indica) and 21 (japonica) associations correspond to truly species-specific TIPs (completely absent in one of the two subspecies).
evidence: This is a result from the frequency analysis of TIP-eQTLs.

claim: 56% of the indica-specific TIPs were present in the rufipogon/nivara population.
source: We looked for these TIPs in 82 Oryza rufipogon and Oryza nivara varieties and found that 56% of the indica-specific and 24% of the japonica-specific TIPs were present in such population.
evidence: This is a result from the analysis of TIP presence in wild rice populations.
